name: Tichurong
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.
catalog_citation: Budha, Jag Bahadur, Maya Daurio & Mark Turin. 2021. Tichurong (Nepal) – Language Snapshot. Language Documentation and Description 20, 189–197. doi:10.25894/ldd50 (open access, lddjournal.org, CC-BY-NC)
catalog_quote: In March 2021, the Nepal Magar Writers Association in Kathmandu hosted a study seminar facilitated by two linguists, Amrit Yonjan Tamang and Tara Mani Rai, to identify phonological and morphological features of Tichurong. ... Tamang and Rai’s preliminary findings identified 35 consonant phonemes, including six major vowels, six nasal vowels, six long vowels, and noted the following significant features of Tichurong: 1. verbs do not exhibit complex conjugational morphology, and there is no verb agreement either by person or by number; 2. there is no gender agreement; 3. it is consistently ergative: the subject of intransitive verbs and object of transitive verbs behave the same; 4. it is tonal.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (10 pp; extracted text page 8 = printed p.195, section 3 'Available resources'). The quoted passage is there word for word; the compiler '..' elide only the sentence 'Together with Honda's survey, this lays the foundations for a better understanding of the genetic affiliation of the language.' and the gloss inside item 3 ('the subject of intransitive verbs and object of transitive verbs behave the same'). The list ends '4. it is tonal.' and the article has no phonology section of its own; the tonal claim is explicitly attributed to Tamang & Rai's unpublished March 2021 Nepal Magar Writers Association seminar findings, so 'statement reported second-hand only' is the right status and '…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible phonological claim is that Tichurong is tonal (reported second-hand from an unpublished 2021 seminar); no source says anything about word stress or its position. Tournadre & Suzuki (2023: 581) generalise that all Tibetic groups of northern Nepal have a two-way (high/low) pitch tone system, again without a stress statement for this variety.
new_statements.domain_note: No stress domain discussed; the tonal claim is a bare typological flag with no detail on tone-bearing unit or word-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources treat the same variety: the Tibetic dialect of the Tichurong valley (Thuli Bheri, Dolpa), called Tichyurong Tibetan by Honda, Poike/Poinke/Rongke/Tichurongke locally (tich1238, ISO tcn). Not to be confused with Kaike (kaik1246), the non-Tibetic language of five villages in the same valley, nor with Dolpo (dolp1238), its closest relative, for which Kopp (2011) exists. Tournadre & Suzuki group 'Dölpo and Tichyurong' as one dialect group of the SW section.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. p.195 reports second-hand the preliminary findings of a March 2021 Nepal Magar Writers Association seminar (Amrit Yonjan Tamang & Tara Mani Rai): 35 consonant phonemes, six oral/six nasal/six long vowels, no verb agreement, ergative, and '4. it is tonal.'

sources.citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages: an introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan. Villejuif: LACITO Publications (Part 2).
sources.note: No Tichyurong-specific statement. p.576: 'A neighboring dialect called Tichyurong has been reported by Honda (2018).' Section 9.8.6 (p.581), for the whole SW section: 'All the Tibetic groups of northern Nepal have a pitch tone system usually with a two-way contrast (high and low).' Sec. 7.3.3 says a stress distinction in Tibetic is attested mainly in Balti (family-level, not about Tichyurong).
